analysis.one_liner: Bans partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts, prohibits mid-decade redistricting, and requires public map-drawing.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts and stop mid-decade redistricting never got a hearing or vote, dying in the Senate Judiciary Committee after only its introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set nationwide rules for drawing congressional districts: maps could not be drawn to materially favor one political party, states could redraw maps only once per decade, and districts would have to protect voters' rights under the Voting Rights Act and keep communities together. It would require open public hearings, published data, and public map-drawing tools, and if a state missed its deadline, a three-judge federal court would draw the map instead. States that defied the rules could be sued by the Attorney General or by their own voters.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters whose ballots are currently diluted by gerrymandered districts, including racial and language minority voters who would gain stronger protections under the bill's Voting Rights Act criteria, and communities of interest that are currently split across districts. More competitive districts would also make more House seats responsive to ordinary voters instead of party map-drawers.

how_it_helps.text: Bans any congressional map drawn with the intent or effect of materially favoring or disfavoring a political party, with a quantitative test using the two most recent presidential and Senate elections to flag unfair maps.
Prohibits mid-decade redistricting, so a state could redraw its map only once after each census unless a court orders it, closing off partisan re-draws between elections.

Strengthens protections for minority voters by requiring districts where protected groups, including two or more groups acting in coalition, have a practical ability to elect representatives of their choice.

Forces map-drawing into the open: public hearings before and after proposed maps are released, a public website with all data, maps, comments, and free software for citizens to draw their own proposals, notices in covered languages, and a written fairness evaluation at least 48 hours before any vote.
Bar map-drawers from considering where incumbent members of Congress live, removing the most direct incumbent-protection tool.

Creates real enforcement: if a state misses its map deadline, a three-judge federal court takes over and draws the map, and the Attorney General or any affected voter can sue, with courts empowered to impose replacement maps in time for the next election.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress in safe gerrymandered seats and the legislators and party operatives who draw the maps would lose control over district boundaries and the ability to entrench their side. State governments would bear the cost of the transparency requirements, litigation in which courts may award attorney's fees against the state, and court-drawn maps if they miss deadlines.

drawbacks.text: If a state misses its deadline, an unelected three-judge court, possibly aided by a special master, would draw the congressional map, shifting a political decision out of elected hands.

States with existing non-compliant maps would have only 45 days after enactment to redraw them, and a filed lawsuit automatically freezes use of a challenged map, which could force disruptive mid-cycle map changes close to elections.

The partisan-fairness test relies on contested quantitative measures such as the efficiency gap; a plan exceeding a threshold in just two of four elections triggers a presumption of violation, inviting heavy litigation over statistical methods that courts and experts disagree about.
The bill covers only congressional districts, leaving state legislative gerrymandering untouched, so much of the map-drawing problem would remain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — a ban on partisan gerrymandering, a once-per-decade limit, minority-vote protections, and genuinely public map-drawing — address a real problem: members of Congress currently choose their voters. The costs are real but mostly procedural: heavy reliance on courts to draw maps, a rushed 45-day deadline for existing maps, and litigation over statistical fairness measures. A reasonable supporter would concede the court-centered enforcement design is complex and could create short-term disruption, but the bill's safeguards, like interim plans and expedited review, are attempts to manage that disruption rather than ignore it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the Redistricting Reform Act of 2024 in the Senate on February 7, 2024, joined by Senator Laphonza Butler.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill had only one cosponsor besides its sponsor, so it lacked the committee support that would normally pressure a chair to schedule it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress in safe gerrymandered districts, and the legislators and party operatives who draw the maps, keep the ability to choose their voters for another decade. No state had to redraw a map or open its process under the bill's rules.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, which set anti-gerrymandering criteria, banned mid-decade redistricting, and created court and public enforcement mechanisms.

for.name: Laphonza Butler
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the only additional supporter in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Dick Durbin, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 7, 2024 and took no further action on it in the record; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; because it never cleared committee, it was never eligible for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only senators on record were both Democrats, and no Republican sponsored or publicly supported the bill in the record.

industries.note: The bill bans considering where incumbents live and bans maps that materially favor one party, ending the safe-seat protection that gerrymandering gives most House members. Their interest in keeping maps they drew runs directly against voters' interest in competitive, fair districts.

State legislators and the party operatives who draw congressional maps would lose control of the process, face public hearings and published data, and could have maps replaced by a federal court if they miss deadlines. Their control over district boundaries is what the bill exists to limit.
